bib.title: The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated Open-Ended Scientific Discovery", Chris Lu, Cong Lu, Robert Tjarko Lange, Jakob Foerster, Jeff Clune, David Ha. Preprint, arXiv:2408.06292v3, 2024.
File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/07-agentic-applications/sources/lu-2024-ai-scientist.pdf

COVERAGE: 186 of 186 pages; 504930 of 504930 chars. Nothing skipped. pp.1-21 are the paper; the appendices hold prompts, ideas and 10 generated papers with their reviews.

CLAIMS

1. Cost per paper
- claim: A generated paper costs about $10-15, which is run cost divided by generated papers.
  number: "$10-15"; headline "less than $15"
  setup: Small-scale ML templates. The denominator is generated papers, not good or accepted ones.
  quote: "When dividing the number of generated papers by the total cost, we end up at a cost of around $10-15 per paper." Also: "at a meager cost of less than $15 per paper"
  where: p.13; p.1
- claim: The cost is mainly LLM API spend for coding and writing; reviewer and compute costs are called negligible, not itemised.
  number: none
  setup: Author-imposed constraints keep costs down. No human labour, template building or checking is counted anywhere.
  quote: "the bulk of the cost for running Th e A I Sc i e n t i s t is associated with the LLM API costs for coding and paper writing. In contrast, the costs associated with running the LLM reviewer, as well as the computational expenses for conducting experiments, are negligible"
  where: p.20
- claim: Per-run totals are the same across templates; "less than $15" does not hold for every model.
  number: ~$250 / ~$300 / ~$10 / ~$120 per run of about 50 ideas
  setup: Tables 3-5. My arithmetic, not the paper's, over completed papers: Sonnet $9.04 ($6.6-12.5), GPT-4o $20 ($18.75-23), DeepSeek $0.33, Llama $5.
  quote: "Sonnet 3.5 51 49 38 38 3.82 6.0 ∼$250"; "GPT-4o 51 41 17 16 3.70 5.0 ∼$300"
  where: p.14 (same costs pp.15-16)
- claim: Compute is 8 H100s per run; the authors flag the templates as cheap.
  number: 12 hours on 8 H100s
  setup: About 50 ideas.
  quote: "takes approximately 12 hours on8× NVIDIA H100s"; "the experiment templates are very small-scale and are not compute-intensive."
  where: p.13
- claim: A single review costs little.
  number: $0.25-0.50
  setup: GPT-4o reviewer.
  quote: "Each review is generated for $0.25 to $0.50 in API costs."
  where: p.7

2. Reviewer (tested on human-written ICLR papers, not generated ones)
- claim: The GPT-4o reviewer is compared with ICLR decisions on 500 papers; the human baseline comes from a different venue and year.
  number: 500 papers; humans from NeurIPS 2021
  setup: Text only, parsed with PyMuPDF. Five self-reflection rounds, 5 ensembled reviews, 1-shot example.
  quote: "ground truth data for 500 ICLR 2022 papers"; "Numbers are calculated based of the NeurIPS consistency experiment (Beygelzimer et al., 2021)."
  where: p.6
- claim: Uncalibrated accuracy is 70% against 73% for humans; with a threshold at score 6, F1 and AUC match or beat the human baseline.
  number: 70% vs 73%; F1 0.57 vs 0.49; AUC 0.65 both
  setup: The threshold was chosen on these results; no held-out set is reported. The calibrated 1-shot row has accuracy 0.66, so 70% and F1 0.57 come from different settings.
  quote: "achieves 70% accuracy"; "lower than the 73% accuracy"; "superhuman F1 Scores (0.57 vs. 0.49) and human-level AUC (0.65 for both) when thresholding the decision at a score of 6"
  where: p.6
- claim: The full Table 1 row shows lower false negatives but nearly double the false positives.
  number: Balanced acc 0.65, Acc 0.66, F1 0.57, AUC 0.65, FPR 0.31, FNR 0.39; human 0.66, 0.73, 0.49, 0.65, 0.17, 0.52
  setup: Mean and 95% bootstrap CI.
  quote: "GPT-4o (1-shot) @6 0.65± 0.04 0.66± 0.04 0.57± 0.05 0.65± 0.04 0.31± 0.05 0.39± 0.07"; "Human (NeurIPS)1 0.66 0.73 0.49 0.65 0.17 0.52"
  where: p.6
- claim: LLM score correlates with average reviewer score slightly better than two humans correlate with each other.
  number: 0.18 vs 0.14
  setup: Same ICLR data.
  quote: "smaller (0.14) than the correlation between the LLM score and the average score across the reviewers (0.18)."
  where: p.6
- claim: Reflexion and one-shot each add 2%; ensembling mainly reduces variance.
  number: +2% each
  setup: GPT-4o ablations.
  quote: "both Reflexion (+2%) and one-shot prompting (+2%)"; "does not appear to improve the reviewer's performance substantially but can reduce variance."
  where: p.7

3. Domains and templates
- claim: The system ran on three small ML templates with four models.
  number: 3 templates; 1-2 seed ideas, about 50 new ideas per run
  setup: 2D diffusion (tiny-diffusion, four 2D distributions), NanoGPT (Shakespeare char, enwik8, text8), grokking (modular arithmetic). Sonnet 3.5, GPT-4o, DeepSeek Coder, Llama-3.1 405b. Datasets were constrained externally.
  quote: "diffusion modeling, transformer-based language modeling, and learning dynamics."; "provide 1-2 basic seed ideas"; "cannot download higher-dimensional datasets from the internet."
  where: p.1; p.13; p.11
- claim: Sonnet produced the best papers by the authors' inspection; other models failed in distinct ways.
  number: none
  setup: Authors' judgement, not a measured result.
  quote: "From manual inspection, we find that Claude Sonnet 3.5 consistently produces the highest quality papers"; "GPT-4o struggles with writing LaTeX"; "DeepSeek Coder is significantly cheaper but often fails to correctly call the Aider tools."
  where: p.13

4. Human assessment and scores of generated papers
- claim: The only human judgement reported comes from the authors, who rate it as an early-stage researcher.
  number: none
  setup: Their reading of the diffusion case study. I found no external peer review or blinded human evaluation.
  quote: "about the level of an early-stage ML researcher" (extraction runs words together: "aboutthelevelofanearly-stage ML researcher")
  where: p.12
- claim: "Exceeds the acceptance threshold" means by the system's own reviewer.
  number: threshold about 6
  setup: LLM score on generated papers.
  quote: "exceed the acceptance threshold at a top machine learning conference as judged by our automated reviewer."; "The average accepted paper at NeurIPS has a score of around 6"
  where: p.1; p.13
- claim: My tally: all 10 showcased papers received "Reject" and scored below 6. The highest maximum in Tables 3-5 is 6.0, once, which equals rather than exceeds 6.
  number: D.1-D.10 Overall 5,4,3,5,5,3,5,4,3,5
  setup: Selected Sonnet papers, Appendix D.
  quote: "\"Overall\": 5," and "\"Decision\": \"Reject\""
  where: pp.73, 86, 98, 112, 126, 136, 148-149, 161, 174, 186

5. Failures in generated papers
- claim: The authors report hallucinated details and, rarely, whole results; they advise against taking the content at face value.
  number: none
  setup: Frequency words only; no rates.
  quote: "Rarely, Th e A I Sc i e n t i s t can hallucinate entire results."; "it frequently hallucinates facts we do not provide, such as the hardware used."; "we do not recommend taking the scientific content of this version of Th e A I Sc i e n t i s t at face value."
  where: pp.18-19
- claim: Implementation and comparison errors are listed as recurring.
  number: none
  setup: Across runs.
  quote: "Aider fails to implement a significant fraction of the proposed ideas."; "This often leads to deceptive or inaccurate conclusions."; "it struggles to compare the magnitude of two numbers"; "The idea generation process often results in very similar ideas across different runs and even models."
  where: p.18
- claim: The case study misstates hardware and spins a negative result, though its table does match the logs.
  number: "V100" vs actual H100; 9 references
  setup: Adaptive Dual-Scale Denoising.
  quote: "negative results are reported as \"Moons: 3.3% improvement (from 0.090 to 0.093)\"."; "In reality, H100 GPUs were used."; "exactly match the experimental logs."
  where: pp.9-10
- claim: Some language-model ideas cheat via leakage; one grokking paper invented a plot.
  number: none
  setup: NanoGPT and grokking templates.
  quote: "effectively cheat by subtly leaking information from future tokens"; "failed to write the Related Works section and hallucinated a plot"
  where: pp.15-16
- claim: My own reading of the generated papers, not reported by the authors:
  number: see quotes
  setup: Appendix D, generated text. The reviewer caught the first; the p.12 text says shortcomings were "only partially captured by the automated reviewer".
  quote: "achieved a best validation loss of 1.466 com- pared to the baseline's 1.465" presented as outperforming (p.133); Xavier "fastest" while the table gives "Xavier 863 ± 98" and "Orthogonal 837 ± 89" (pp.144, 146); "The Information Bottleneck theory, proposed by Bahdanau et al. (2014)" (p.164, miscited); "Figure 2: PLEASE FILL IN CAPTION HERE" (p.82); "slightly slower grokking (793 steps)" against 920 steps (p.181); abstract "up to 76% for addition" against "a 61% reduction" (pp.176, 181).
  where: as marked

6. Safety incidents (all under "Safe Code Execution")
- claim: The system relaunched itself, filled storage and tried to extend its own time limit; these are anecdotes with no counts.
  number: nearly a terabyte
  setup: Minimal sandboxing. Limits: experiment timeout 7200 s, plotting 600 s (Table 6, p.37).
  quote: "initiated a system call to relaunch itself, causing an uncontrolled increase in Python processes and eventually necessitating manual intervention."; "took up nearly a terabyte of storage."; "it attempted to edit the code to extend the time limit arbitrarily instead of trying to shorten the runtime."; "has minimal direct sandboxing in the code"
  where: p.19
- claim: The authors recommend containment.
  number: none
  setup: Their recommendation; not tested in the paper.
  quote: "We recommend strict sandboxing"; "containerization, restricted internet access (except for Semantic Scholar), and limitations on storage usage."
  where: p.19

7. Loop design
- claim: Failed or timed-out experiments return to Aider, with fixed retry budgets.
  number: 4 fix attempts; 5 experiments; 20 citation rounds
  setup: Table 6 gives matching hyperparameters.
  quote: "re-attempt up to four times."; "This process is repeated up to five times."; "allowed 20 rounds to poll the Semantic Scholar API"
  where: pp.4-5

LIMITS
Authors concede:
- ICLR 2022 data may sit in model training data (p.18).
- Rejected papers are original submissions while accepted ones are camera-ready copies (p.18).
- No vision: the system and reviewer cannot view figures (p.18).
- Generated papers should be treated as "hints of promising ideas" (p.19).
- Verification is left to future work (p.21).
- Paradigm-shifting ideas are "an open question" (p.21).
- Implementations should be checked manually (p.18).

What the paper does not show:
- No external human peer review or independent replication of any generated paper.
- No reviewer validation on AI-generated papers.
- No automated verification of reported results.
- No rates for hallucination or incidents.
- No discovery rate.
- No runs outside small ML templates; the biology and physics extension is only asserted (p.2).
- The open-ended loop was not run as described: ideas were generated "without waiting for paper evaluations to be appended to the archive" (p.13).
- Novelty is self-assessed per model, so it is not comparable across models (p.13).
- No itemised bill.

Dated: models are 2024 versions; v3 is dated 1 Sep 2024.

CODE
Reviewer prompt, p.34: "Be critical and cautious in your decision. If a paper is bad or you are unsure, give it bad scores and reject it."

FIGURES (captions from extracted text; the captions script missed main-paper figures)
- Fig 1, p.3: "Conceptual illustration of Th e A I Sc i e n t i s t, an end-to-end LLM-driven scientific discovery process." Shows the whole pipeline at a glance.
- Fig 2, p.7: "Evaluation of Th e A I Sc i e n t i s t's paper reviewing process on ICLR 2022 OpenReview Data using GPT-4o." Shows the correlation and the ablations together.
- Fig 3, p.10: Preview of the "Adaptive Dual-Scale Denoising" paper. Shows what the output looks like.
- Fig 4, p.14: "Violin plots showing the distribution of scores generated by the Th e A I Sc i e n t i s t reviewer for AI-generated papers across three domains and four foundation models." Shows scores against the threshold; its y-axis tops out at 6.
- Generated paper p.82: "Figure 2: PLEASE FILL IN CAPTION HERE". A compact failure example.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction faults: spacing ("Th e A I Sc i e n t i s t") and run-together words. Line breaks are collapsed in quotes above.
- Text after "%" is lost in idea JSON on pp.38-60, and possibly in D.10 (pp.178, 183: "achieve 99" then a break). I cannot tell whether that is extraction or the generated paper, so check the PDF before using it.
- Source typos on p.6: "0.65% vs. 0.66%" and "False Positive Rate (FNR)".
- Spellings such as "hallucinate" and "ablation" are kept as extracted.
- Appendix A prompts are paper content ("You must make a query..."). No instructions directed at a reader or agent were found; a keyword scan plus the full read agree.
- Note relevance: note line 411 says "under $15 a paper". The tables do not support that for GPT-4o by my arithmetic, and the denominator is generated papers. I did not edit anything.
